lesson.title: Code Your Own CLI With Rust: a Better ls
lesson.goal: build a command-line tool in Rust with cargo that parses arguments

sources.title: Code Your Own CLI With Rust: a Better ls

steps.title: Create project and parse args
steps.instructions: Run `cargo new best_ls`, add `clap = { version = "4.5.39", features = ["derive"] }` to Cargo.toml, and define `#[derive(Parser)] struct Cli { path: Option<PathBuf> }` with `let cli = Cli::parse();` in main. Run `cargo run -- -h` to see the generated help.

targets.caption: Add clap with the derive feature
Define the Cli struct deriving Parser

explanations.topic: clap derive feature makes argument parsing easy
Option<PathBuf> as the first positional argument
#[derive(Parser)] adds the parse method
Using -- to pass arguments through cargo run

hints: Make sure clap is listed under [dependencies] in Cargo.toml with features = ["derive"].
Your struct needs #[derive(Parser)] and `use clap::Parser;` at the top of main.rs.
Import PathBuf with `use std::path::PathBuf;` and make the field `path: Option<PathBuf>`.
Run `cargo run -- -h`. The `--` separates cargo's flags from your program's flags.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the derive feature on clap, which causes 'cannot find derive macro Parser'.
Forgetting `use clap::Parser;`, which makes `Cli::parse()` fail to resolve.
Running `cargo run -h` without `--`, which shows cargo's help instead of your app's help.
Not importing std::path::PathBuf.
An unused variable warning for `cli` is expected and is not an error.

steps.title: Add version and about metadata
steps.instructions: Annotate your clap Parser struct with `#[command(version, about, long_about = "...")]`. Check with `cargo run -- --version` and `cargo run -- -h`.

targets.caption: Add the command attribute above the struct

explanations.topic: #[command(version)] auto-adds a --version flag from Cargo.toml
Help output now lists the version flag
about and long_about fill in the help description

hints: Clap reads metadata from an attribute placed right above your #[derive(Parser)] struct.
Add #[command(version, about, long_about = "...")] directly above the struct definition.
Pass flags to your program after `--`: `cargo run -- --version`, then `cargo run -- -h`.
If `about` shows nothing, add a `description` in Cargo.toml or a doc comment on the struct.
common_mistakes: Running `cargo run --version`, which prints cargo's version instead of your tool's (missing `--`).
Writing #[clap(...)] / #[command] without enabling clap's `derive` feature.
Putting the attribute above `fn main` instead of the struct.
Spelling it `longabout` or `long-about` instead of `long_about`.
Forgetting quotes around the long_about string.

steps.title: Default the path argument
steps.instructions: Add `let path = cli.path.unwrap_or(PathBuf::from("."));` and print it with `path.display()`. Run `cargo run -- long_path` and `cargo run` to see it print the path or `.`.

targets.caption: Default the optional path to the current directory

explanations.topic: cli.path is an Option, so unwrap_or supplies a default
Defaulting to '.' means the current directory, like ls
Running with and without an argument prints the path or '.'

hints: cli.path is an Option<PathBuf>; use a method that falls back to a default value.
Write let path = cli.path.unwrap_or(PathBuf::from("."));
PathBuf doesn't implement Display directly. Print it with println!("{}", path.display());
Pass arguments after `--`: cargo run -- long_path. Then run plain cargo run to see '.'.
common_mistakes: Forgetting `use std::path::PathBuf;` so PathBuf is not found.
Trying println!("{}", path) without .display(), which fails because PathBuf doesn't implement Display.
Running `cargo run long_path` without `--`, so the argument goes to cargo instead of your program.
Using unwrap() instead of unwrap_or, which panics when no path is given.
Declaring path as PathBuf instead of Option<PathBuf> in the Cli struct, so unwrap_or doesn't exist.

steps.title: Check path existence with colors
steps.instructions: Use `if let Ok(does_exist) = fs::exists(&path)` and print "Path does not exist" in red via owo-colors when false, "Error reading directory" on error. Add `owo-colors` to Cargo.toml and run with a nonexistent path.

targets.caption: Check whether the given path exists
Red error for a missing path

explanations.topic: fs::exists reports whether a path exists
owo-colors crate for colored terminal output
cargo build puts the debug executable in target/debug
fs::exists returns Err when existence can't be confirmed or denied

hints: Use `if let Ok(does_exist) = fs::exists(&path)` and branch on the bool inside.
Add `owo-colors` under [dependencies] in Cargo.toml (or run `cargo add owo-colors`).
Bring the trait into scope with `use owo_colors::OwoColorize;` so `"text".red()` works.
Handle the else branch of the if let by printing "Error reading directory", then run `cargo run -- not_a_real_path`.
common_mistakes: Forgetting `use owo_colors::OwoColorize;`, so `.red()` is reported as no method found.
Writing `owo_colors` with an underscore in Cargo.toml; the crate name uses a hyphen.
Passing `path` by value to fs::exists and then getting a use-after-move error later; pass `&path`.
Running `cargo run nonexistent` without `--`, which can make cargo consume flag-style arguments.
Using an older Rust toolchain where `std::fs::exists` isn't stable yet (needs Rust 1.81+).

steps.title: List directory file names
steps.instructions: Write `fn get_files(path: &Path) -> Vec<String>` that iterates `fs::read_dir(path)` and collects each `file_name().into_string()`. Loop over it in main, print each name, then `cargo run`.

targets.caption: Helper that collects file names from a directory
cargo run lists the current directory

explanations.topic: Returning a Vec<String> of file names from a helper function
Using if let Ok(...) on fs::read_dir to handle errors
Each directory entry is a Result, unwrapped with another if let
OsString::into_string can fail, so fall back with unwrap_or
No path argument defaults to the current working directory

hints: Write a separate function that takes &Path and returns Vec<String>, then call it from main where the path is known to exist.
fs::read_dir(path) returns a Result. Wrap it in `if let Ok(read_dir) = ...`, then loop over it. Each entry is also a Result.
file.file_name() gives an OsString. Call .into_string(), which returns a Result, and recover with .unwrap_or("unknown name".into()).
In main: `for file in get_files(&path) { println!("{}", file); }` then run `cargo run` with no arguments.
common_mistakes: Forgetting `use std::fs;` or `use std::path::Path;`, which causes unresolved import or name errors.
Passing `path` instead of `&path` to get_files, so the PathBuf is moved or the types don't match.
Calling `.into_string()` and then `.unwrap_or("unknown name")` without `.into()`, which gives a &str/String type mismatch.
Declaring the vector without `mut`, so `push` fails to compile.
Putting the loop in the error branch instead of the branch where the path exists.

steps.title: Collect file metadata into structs
steps.instructions: Add a `FileEntry` struct and a strum `#[derive(Debug, Display)] enum EntryType { File, Dir }`, fill entries from `fs::metadata(file.path())` in a `map_data` function. Pretty-print the entries with `{:#?}` and run `cargo run`.

targets.caption: Data structure holding each file's metadata
Mapping extracted into its own function

explanations.topic: Designing a struct to hold file metadata
Why 'type' can't be a field name (reserved keyword)
Using strum's Display derive for enums
fs::metadata returns Result, so match Ok with if let
Bug: passing the dir path instead of file.path()
Extracting the mapping into map_data

hints: Define a FileEntry struct and an EntryType enum (File, Dir), and derive Debug on both so {:#?} can print them.
Add strum (with the derive feature) to Cargo.toml and use strum::Display to derive Display on EntryType.
Inside the loop, use `if let Ok(meta) = fs::metadata(&file.path())`, then set e_type from meta.is_dir() and len_bytes from meta.len().
Move that block into a `fn map_data(file: fs::DirEntry, data: &mut Vec<FileEntry>)` and print the Vec with println!("{:#?}", ...).
common_mistakes: Passing the directory `path` to fs::metadata instead of `file.path()`, which gives every entry the same type and size.
Naming the field `type`, a reserved keyword. Use `e_type` instead.
Forgetting #[derive(Debug)] on FileEntry or EntryType, so {:#?} fails to compile.
Matching `Some(meta)` instead of `Ok(meta)`: fs::metadata returns a Result, not an Option.
Not enabling strum's `derive` feature (or not adding strum_macros), so the Display derive can't be found.

steps.title: Render a colored table
steps.instructions: Add the `tabled` crate, derive `Tabled` on FileEntry, build `Table::new(get_files(&path))`, apply `Style::rounded()` and color columns/rows with `table.modify(...)`. Rename headers with `#[tabled(rename = ...)]` and run `cargo run`.

targets.caption: Run and see the rounded table

explanations.topic: What the tabled crate does: print structs as ASCII tables
Applying a table style (rounded)
table.modify targets columns/rows to apply colors
#[tabled(rename)] to change header names

hints: Add tabled to Cargo.toml (cargo add tabled) and derive Tabled on FileEntry.
Replace the print loop with let mut table = Table::new(get_files(&path)); then println!("{}", table).
Style and color: table.with(Style::rounded()); table.modify(Columns::first(), Color::FG_BRIGHT_CYAN); use Rows::first() for the header.
Rename headers with #[tabled(rename = "Name")] above each struct field.
common_mistakes: Forgetting #[derive(Tabled)] on FileEntry, or on a field type (an enum) that doesn't implement Display.
Not declaring table as mut before calling with/modify.
Importing Style from the wrong module (there are several Style types); use tabled::settings::Style.
Missing the tabled dependency in Cargo.toml so `use tabled` fails to compile.
Indexing columns from 1 instead of 0 so the wrong column gets colored.

steps.title: Format modified date with chrono
steps.instructions: Add `chrono`, and in map_data use `if let Ok(modi) = meta.modified()` to convert into `DateTime<Utc>` and format it with `date.format("%a %b %e %Y")`, else an empty string. Run `cargo run -- src` to see dates.

targets.caption: Run cargo run -- src and see dates

explanations.topic: Why the chrono crate is needed for dates/times
if let Ok / else fallback to an empty string
meta.modified() returns a Result<SystemTime>
Converting SystemTime into DateTime<Utc> via into()
Format specifiers in date.format()

hints: Add chrono to [dependencies] in Cargo.toml, then find where map_data sets the modified field.
meta.modified() returns a Result<SystemTime>. Use `if let Ok(modi) = meta.modified() { ... } else { String::new() }`.
Inside the Ok branch: `let date: DateTime<Utc> = modi.into();` then `date.format("%a %b %e %Y").to_string()`. Import with `use chrono::{DateTime, Utc};`.
Run `cargo run -- src` and check the Modified column shows dates like 'Mon Jun 3 2024'.
common_mistakes: Naming the binding `mod`, which is a reserved keyword in Rust. Use `modi` or similar.
Forgetting `use chrono::{DateTime, Utc};`, causing 'cannot find type DateTime' errors.
Calling .into() without annotating the type `DateTime<Utc>`, so the compiler can't infer the target.
Not adding chrono to Cargo.toml, giving an 'unresolved import chrono' error.
Leaving off the else branch, so the if-let expression has mismatched types instead of returning a String.

steps.title: Add a JSON output flag
steps.instructions: Add `#[arg(short, long)] json: bool` to Cli in src/main.rs, move table printing into `print_table`, and when `cli.json` print `serde_json::to_string(&get_files(&path))`. Add serde (derive) and serde_json to Cargo.toml, derive `Serialize` on FileEntry and EntryType, then run `cargo run -- -j` and `cargo run -- --json`.

targets.caption: Table printing extracted into its own function
Serialize derived on FileEntry and EntryType
Running with the JSON flag prints entries as JSON

explanations.topic: #[arg(short, long)] gives a flag both -j and --json forms
serde with derive plus serde_json serialize structs to JSON
Every nested type (the EntryType enum) must also derive Serialize
unwrap_or gives a fallback string if serialization fails

hints: Add a `json: bool` field to your Cli struct and put `#[arg(short, long)]` above it, then check `cargo run -- --help` lists -j/--json.
Run `cargo add serde --features derive` and `cargo add serde_json`, then `use serde::Serialize;` and add Serialize to the derive on both FileEntry and EntryType.
Move the table code into `fn print_table(path: PathBuf)` and branch: `if cli.json { ... } else { print_table(path); }`.
In the JSON branch: `println!("{}", serde_json::to_string(&get_files(&path)).unwrap_or("cannot parse json".to_string()));`
common_mistakes: Declaring `json: bool` without `#[arg(short, long)]`, so clap treats it as a positional argument instead of a flag.
Deriving Serialize on FileEntry but not on EntryType, which fails with 'the trait Serialize is not implemented'.
Adding serde without the `derive` feature, so `#[derive(Serialize)]` cannot be found.
Running `cargo run -j` instead of `cargo run -- -j`, so cargo, not your program, receives the flag.
Passing the table (or a moved `path`) to serde_json instead of the Vec returned by get_files.
